uncited: - The input $x$ is a 3D array of voxel intensities.
- The filter $D$ is a 3D array of complex coefficients matching the frequency domain dimensions.
- The noise term $n$ is a 3D array of the same shape as the output $y$.
**Forward Transform:** Compute the 3D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of the input volume $x$ to obtain the high-resolution frequency representation $F_{HR}(x)$.
**Filtering:** Multiply the frequency representation by the low-pass filter $D$.
This operation eliminates high-frequency components that would cause aliasing upon downsampling.
**Inverse Transform:** Compute the inverse FFT of the filtered frequency data, but using the grid parameters of the low-resolution regime.
This yields the spatial domain representation at the lower resolution.
**Noise Addition:** Add a noise term $n$ to the result to produce the final output $y$.
- **Boundary Effects:** FFT assumes periodic boundary conditions.
If the volume has sharp discontinuities at the boundaries, ringing artifacts may occur.
- **Time Complexity:** Dominated by the FFT operations, which are $O(N \log N)$ where $N$ is the number of voxels.
- **Memory Complexity:** Requires storage for the input volume, the frequency domain representation (complex numbers, so 2x memory for real input), the filter, and the output volume.
It is part of an end-to-end architecture that includes an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) and a Super-Resolution (SR) module.
